headline: US and Iran reignite their war over the Strait of Hormuz: Trump drops a 20% shipping fee but presses a naval blockade as strikes fly, pushing oil to a one-month high.
the_big_picture: The single thread running through today is the re-escalation of the US-Iran conflict at the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil. Trump backed off a threatened 20% transit fee but is pushing ahead with a naval blockade while both sides trade strikes and tankers come under attack, sending crude to a one-month high. That oil spike is the hinge for everything downstream: US inflation cooled to 3.5% but officials flagged fresh upside risk, India's inflation just breached its central bank's target, the rupee slid past 96 and the Sensex fell. Running underneath, an AI storyline cuts both ways: IBM shed roughly $70bn in a day after stumbling on AI deals, even as China's AI-driven exports jumped 27% and Nvidia began shipping powerful H200 chips into China.

stories.title: The Fed's two-day meeting starts today — traders now think a rate hold is more likely than a cut
key_points: The **Federal Reserve's policy meeting runs July 28-29**, with a decision due Wednesday.
Markets now price roughly a **64% chance the Fed holds rates steady**, down sharply from an 87% chance just a week ago.
The Fed's target range has sat at **3.50%-3.75%** since its last move.
New Fed Chair **Kevin Warsh** has already changed how the Fed communicates — dropping traditional forward guidance for a **pure 'data-dependent' approach**, making each meeting harder to predict.
US inflation (CPI) rose **4.2% over the year to May 2026**, the biggest 12-month jump since April 2023 — well above the Fed's usual 2% comfort zone.
stories.background: The Federal Reserve is the US central bank — it sets the short-term interest rate that ripples through mortgages, credit cards, business loans, and, because the US dollar and Treasury market are the anchor of global finance, borrowing costs worldwide including in India. Earlier this year the Fed brought in a new chair, Kevin Warsh, who has shifted the Fed's style: instead of pre-signaling what it plans to do next ("forward guidance"), the Fed now says it will decide meeting-by-meeting based purely on incoming data. That makes each Fed decision, including this one, more of a genuine toss-up for markets than it used to be.
stories.what_happened: The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) — the group of officials who set US interest rates — began its scheduled two-day meeting today, with the rate decision due tomorrow, July 29. Going into the meeting, futures markets (where traders bet on what the Fed will do) put the odds of a **hold at rates unchanged around 64%**, a sharp shift from just a week earlier when a hold looked far more certain at 87%. That shift reflects genuine uncertainty: inflation is running hot, with the Consumer Price Index up **4.2% year-over-year through May 2026** — the sharpest annual rise since April 2023 — which normally argues for the Fed to keep rates high or even raise them. But there are also signs of a softening labor market pulling in the opposite direction, toward a cut. The rate has held at **3.50%-3.75%** since the last change, and Warsh's shift away from forward guidance means officials aren't tipping their hand before Wednesday.
stories.why_it_matters: The Fed's rate decision is one of the single biggest swing factors for global markets — it affects how expensive it is to borrow everywhere, how attractive the US dollar is versus other currencies (including the rupee), and how much money flows into or out of emerging markets like India. A surprise cut or hold can move stocks, bonds, gold, and currencies worldwide within minutes of the announcement.
stories.ripple_effects: If the Fed holds rates steady with hawkish (inflation-focused) language, expect the dollar to strengthen and pressure on emerging-market currencies like the rupee, plus higher US Treasury yields pulling money away from riskier assets. If it leans toward signaling a future cut, expect the opposite — a weaker dollar, rally in gold, and relief for import-heavy economies. Indian markets, which already moved on Fed-adjacent oil and rate expectations this week, will be watching closely.
stories.why_now: This is a regularly scheduled meeting (the Fed meets roughly every six weeks), but it's landing at an unusually contested moment — hot inflation data pulling one way, a wobblier jobs picture pulling the other, and a new Fed chair whose communication style has made the outcome genuinely unpredictable rather than pre-telegraphed.
stories.watch_next: The rate decision and Chair Warsh's press conference on Wednesday, July 29, including any language about the path for the rest of 2026.

key_terms.definition: The group of US Federal Reserve officials who meet roughly every six weeks to set the US interest rate.
When a central bank tells markets in advance roughly what it plans to do at future meetings, so there are fewer surprises — the new Fed chair has moved away from this.
A measure of how much prices for everyday goods and services have risen — the most-watched gauge of inflation.

stories.the_lesson: When a central bank stops giving forward guidance and goes fully 'data-dependent,' every fresh economic report becomes a market-moving event on its own — traders can no longer coast on a pre-announced plan, so volatility around each data release tends to rise.
stories.market_link: US Treasury yields, the dollar index, gold, and — via capital flows — Indian equities, the rupee (USDINR), and RBI's own rate path all react to this decision.

stories.title: US and Iran edge toward a formal ceasefire deal, with the Strait of Hormuz the last sticking point
key_points: Mediators report **real progress** reviving talks after nearly two weeks of direct US-Iran fighting.
The sketched compromise would let Iran manage ship traffic through the **Strait of Hormuz** with **fewer restrictions**, instead of the US demanding open access outright.
President Trump says Washington paused renewed strikes **at Iran's request**, but warns they resume if no deal is reached.
Iran's Foreign Ministry publicly denies any active negotiations are underway — the two sides are not yet aligned on the basic facts.
Even with a pause, Iran-backed militia drones are still flying: **Saudi Arabia shot down drones** fired at it from Iraq this week.
stories.background: In early July 2026, a rapid escalation between the US and Iran turned into the most direct fighting between the two countries in decades, with US strikes on Iranian targets and Iranian retaliation that spilled into the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which **about a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments pass** every day. Iran responded to strikes by asserting more control over the strait and firing on vessels, which is what sent oil prices spiking and then, on hopes of a ceasefire, tumbling nearly 7% (as covered here yesterday). A truce has technically been holding for over a week, but the two sides have not yet signed anything formal.
stories.what_happened: Regional mediators say they've made genuine headway getting US and Iranian officials back to the table after the fighting paused. The emerging shape of a deal centers on the Strait of Hormuz: rather than Iran ceding full control, it would be allowed to **run vessel-transit management through the strait with fewer restrictions on ships** than the US originally wanted — a face-saving compromise for Tehran. President Trump said the US held off on resuming strikes **because Iran asked it to**, while making clear the US remains ready to hold Iran to account if talks collapse. Muddying the picture, Iran's Foreign Ministry told reporters there are **no current negotiations** taking place — a direct contradiction of the mediators' account. Meanwhile the ceasefire remains fragile in practice: Saudi Arabia intercepted and shot down drones this week fired by Iran-backed militia groups operating out of Iraq, a reminder that the wider network of Iran-aligned armed groups across the region hasn't stood down.
stories.why_it_matters: The Strait of Hormuz is the world's most important oil chokepoint — a real disruption there doesn't just hurt Iran or the US, it moves fuel prices everywhere, including at the pump in India. Whether this ceasefire becomes a real, signed deal or quietly falls apart determines whether that risk stays elevated through the rest of 2026.
stories.ripple_effects: Oil markets are trading on ceasefire headlines almost daily — expect continued volatility in crude prices, and knock-on moves in Indian fuel costs, airline stocks, and inflation forecasts. A durable deal would also ease pressure on global shipping insurers and Gulf state economies; a collapse would risk another spike like the one seen two weeks ago.
stories.why_now: The contradiction between the mediators (who say talks are progressing) and Iran's own Foreign Ministry (which denies any negotiation) is surfacing today because both sides are under pressure to show their own domestic audiences they haven't caved — Iran doesn't want to look like it's negotiating from weakness, while the US wants credit for de-escalating.
stories.watch_next: Whether Iran's Foreign Ministry statement is contradicted or confirmed by an actual signed framework in the coming days — and whether the Strait of Hormuz stays open to shipping without incident.

key_terms.definition: A narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments must pass through — control over it means control over a huge share of global energy supply.
An agreement to stop fighting, which can be informal and shaky (like this one) or later formalized into a signed, binding deal.

stories.the_lesson: In a conflict over a chokepoint like Hormuz, an informal pause in fighting is not the same as peace — prices and markets stay jumpy until there's an actual signed agreement, because a single contradicting statement from either side can undo weeks of de-escalation.
stories.market_link: Crude oil prices (Brent/WTI), Gulf shipping and insurance names, and Indian oil-marketing companies (which import heavily via Hormuz) all move on ceasefire headlines here.

thread.previously: Yesterday, oil prices sank nearly 7% as the ceasefire held and Tehran opened talks on the Strait of Hormuz, with early signs the two sides were moving toward de-escalation.
thread.changed: Today mediators say real progress is being made on a Hormuz vessel-transit compromise, but Iran's own Foreign Ministry is publicly denying any negotiations are happening — and Saudi Arabia just shot down Iran-backed militia drones, showing the ceasefire is still fragile on the ground.

stories.title: Deportation protections for 300,000+ Haitians in the US expire today, and ICE is ready to move
key_points: A federal appeals court's temporary block on ending **Temporary Protected Status (TPS)** for Haitians expires **today, July 27**, clearing the way to strip protections from roughly **300,000 Haitians**.
ICE has been preparing targeted enforcement operations, including in **Ohio**, home to a large Haitian community, with deportation flights reportedly able to begin within days.
The **US Supreme Court** already ruled on **June 25** that the administration could proceed with ending TPS for Haiti and Syria, so today's deadline is the last of three court-ordered delays.
Roughly **145,000** of the affected Haitians live in Florida, including about **36,000** working in health care.
Migrants who leave voluntarily can be offered a government-funded flight home plus a **$2,600** payment.
stories.background: Temporary Protected Status lets people from countries hit by war, disaster, or crisis live and work in the US legally, without a path to citizenship, as long as their home country's designation stays active. Haiti has held TPS for over a decade because of gang violence, political collapse, and a 2021 earthquake that made large parts of the country unsafe to return to. The administration moved to end Haiti's TPS status earlier this year, arguing conditions no longer justify it — a decision challenged in court as endangering people who fled genuine danger. The Supreme Court sided with the administration on **June 25**, but a federal appeals court kept issuing short extensions, pushing the deadline back three times, with today marking the final one's expiry.
stories.what_happened: The US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit's temporary block on revoking Haitian TPS status expires today, after the court pushed the deadline back multiple times since late June while weighing the government's case. Unless a last-minute order intervenes, roughly **300,000 Haitians** living legally in the US under TPS lose that protection and their work permits starting today. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been preparing targeted operations to arrest and deport Haitian migrants, according to internal documents reported by CBS News, with Ohio — home to a large Haitian population in cities like Springfield — identified as an early target. The Supreme Court already cleared the way for this on **June 25**, in a ruling that also stripped protections from about 6,000 Syrians, so today's expiry is procedural rather than a new legal decision. Affected migrants can accept a government-funded flight and a $2,600 payment to leave voluntarily, or risk arrest and forced deportation. An estimated 145,000 of the affected Haitians live in Florida alone, including roughly 36,000 in health care roles.
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the largest single removals of legal status from any immigrant group in recent US history, affecting people who have built homes, jobs, and families in the US for years under a legal program. It also lands on a country many experts say remains genuinely unsafe — Haiti has had no functioning elected government for years and large parts of its capital are controlled by armed gangs.
stories.ripple_effects: US industries that rely on Haitian TPS workers — healthcare, meatpacking, construction — face sudden labor shortages in the communities where they're concentrated, like Springfield, Ohio and South Florida. Haiti itself must absorb a wave of returnees with few jobs or services waiting for them. The move also sets a template for how the administration may treat other countries' TPS holders, including Venezuelans and Hondurans, whose protections face similar legal fights.
stories.why_now: Today is simply the date the courts set — the third and final deadline the DC Circuit granted before its temporary block on the Supreme Court's June ruling runs out.
stories.watch_next: Whether ICE moves quickly on the reported Ohio operations in the coming days, and whether Haitian advocacy groups win any further emergency stay.

key_terms.definition: A US immigration status that lets people from designated crisis-hit countries live and work legally in the US without a path to citizenship, renewed periodically by the government.

stories.the_lesson: A Supreme Court ruling doesn't end a legal fight immediately — lower courts can still grant short delays, so the actual deadline date, not just the headline verdict, is what determines when a policy truly takes effect.

stories.title: Houthi drones strike Saudi Arabia's main east-west oil pipeline, widening the Yemen war's reach into the kingdom's oil backbone
key_points: Yemen's Houthi rebels launched drone strikes today targeting Saudi Arabia's **Petroline**, the pipeline that carries **7 million barrels a day** from eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the strikes hit pumping and transport points, calling it retaliation for **repeated Saudi drone incursions into Yemeni airspace**.
Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Defense said its air defenses **intercepted and destroyed** the attacking drones before any damage.
It follows Houthi strikes on Aramco refineries in **Jizan and Yanbu** days earlier that sent Brent crude above **$100 a barrel**.
The Houthis have also declared a **naval blockade** of Saudi ports this month, marking a sharp escalation from the years-long truce.
stories.background: Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement held an uneasy truce for several years after a brutal civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis seized Yemen's capital Sanaa and a Saudi-led coalition intervened to back the internationally recognized government. That truce unraveled this month after a Saudi strike on Sanaa's airport aimed at stopping an Iranian plane from landing, provoking the Houthis into firing missiles at Saudi Arabia and declaring a **blockade** of its ports. The Houthis are part of Iran's regional network of allied armed groups, and their return to open conflict has opened a new front in the wider **US-Israel-Iran confrontation** that has dominated the region this year. Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure was last hit at this scale roughly four years ago.
stories.what_happened: On Monday, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had launched drone strikes on facilities along Saudi Arabia's East-West crude pipeline, known as Petroline, which moves oil roughly 1,200 km from the kingdom's eastern fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. The pipeline normally runs at its full capacity of **7 million barrels a day** and exists partly so Saudi Arabia can export oil without routing tankers through the Strait of Hormuz. Saree said the attack targeted supply and transport points, framing it as retaliation for repeated Saudi drone flights over Yemeni territory. Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Defense confirmed its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several drones, with no reported casualties or disruption to pipeline flows. This is the third major Houthi strike on Saudi oil infrastructure within a week, after attacks on Aramco's Jizan and Yanbu refineries on July 25 briefly pushed Brent crude above $100 a barrel. Shipping through the nearby Bab el-Mandeb Strait has already fallen to its lowest level in months as vessels avoid the area.
stories.why_it_matters: Petroline exists specifically so Saudi Arabia isn't fully dependent on shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has threatened to close before. If the Houthis can credibly threaten that pipeline too, Saudi Arabia loses its main insurance policy against a Hormuz shutdown — which is why even an intercepted, damage-free strike moves oil markets.
stories.ripple_effects: Sustained attacks raise insurance costs for tankers and pipeline operators, which eventually shows up in fuel prices worldwide. It also pulls Saudi Arabia further into a war it had tried to stay out of since 2022, raising the risk of broader Saudi-Houthi and Saudi-Iran escalation. For India, which imports over 80% of its crude, sustained Gulf instability directly affects fuel costs, inflation, and the rupee.
stories.why_now: The truce that had held for roughly three years collapsed this month after the Saudi strike on Sanaa airport, and the Houthis have escalated in stages since — missiles, a naval blockade, refinery strikes, and now a direct hit on the pipeline that is Saudi Arabia's oil lifeline.
stories.watch_next: Whether Saudi Arabia responds militarily against Houthi positions in Yemen beyond its July 25 airstrikes on Hodeidah.

key_terms.definition: A roughly 1,200-km pipeline carrying Saudi crude from eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, letting the kingdom export oil without sailing tankers through the Strait of Hormuz.
A Yemeni armed political movement, backed by Iran, that controls much of northern Yemen including the capital Sanaa and has fought a Saudi-led coalition since 2014.

stories.the_lesson: When a country builds a backup route for something as critical as oil exports, that backup becomes a target the moment tensions rise — redundancy only protects you until an adversary can reach the redundant path too.
stories.market_link: Brent and WTI crude typically jump on Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure; watch energy stocks, Indian oil-marketing companies exposed to crude swings, and the rupee, which weakens when India's import bill rises.

thread.previously: Houthi strikes on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea sent Brent crude above $100 a barrel for the first time since May, before prices eased back to around $97-98 by July 24.
thread.changed: The Houthis have now struck Saudi Arabia's main East-West pipeline directly rather than tankers at sea — hitting fixed oil infrastructure inside Saudi territory, though Saudi air defenses say they intercepted the drones this time.

stories.title: A NASA astronaut and two Russian cosmonauts land back on Earth after 241 days on the space station
key_points: NASA's Chris Williams and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev landed safely in Kazakhstan on Sunday after **241 days** aboard the International Space Station.
Their Soyuz MS-28 capsule made a parachute-assisted landing near **Zhezkazgan, Kazakhstan**, ending a mission that began on **November 27, 2025**.
The crew orbited Earth **3,856 times**, covering more than **102 million miles**.
It was the first spaceflight for both Williams and Mikaev, and the second for Kud-Sverchkov.
The mission is one of the routine crew rotations that keep the ISS staffed — a partnership that has kept running even as US-Russia relations have soured elsewhere.
stories.background: The International Space Station (ISS) has been continuously crewed by rotating teams of astronauts and cosmonauts since 2000, in a rare corner of US-Russia cooperation that has largely continued through wars and sanctions elsewhere. Crews typically fly up on Russia's Soyuz spacecraft or America's SpaceX Crew Dragon and stay for six months to a year, running science experiments in microgravity that can't be done on Earth. This mission, Soyuz MS-28, launched in late November 2025 and is one of many routine handovers that keep the station running.
stories.what_happened: NASA astronaut Chris Williams and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev returned to Earth on Sunday, July 26, after **241 days** in space aboard the ISS. Their Soyuz MS-28 spacecraft undocked from the station at 2:03am and made a parachute-assisted landing in a remote area southeast of Zhezkazgan, Kazakhstan, at 5:27am CDT (3:27pm local Kazakhstan time). Over the mission, the crew circled the Earth **3,856 times** and travelled more than **102 million miles**. They had launched to the ISS on November 27, 2025. It was the first flight to space for both Williams and Mikaev, while Kud-Sverchkov was on his second mission.
stories.why_it_matters: Every safe crew rotation matters for keeping the ISS — humanity's only continuously crewed outpost in orbit — running, especially as the station ages toward its planned retirement later this decade. It's also a reminder that US-Russia space cooperation has kept functioning as one of the few steady bridges between the two countries amid broader geopolitical tension.
stories.ripple_effects: Williams and his crewmates now face weeks of medical monitoring to help doctors understand how long-duration spaceflight affects the human body — data that feeds directly into planning for future Moon and Mars missions. Their departure also means a new crew has already taken over ISS operations, keeping the research pipeline running without interruption.
stories.why_now: The landing was simply the scheduled end of a roughly eight-month rotation — these handovers happen several times a year to keep the station staffed and give each crew a manageable mission length.
stories.watch_next: NASA's post-flight health assessments of the returning crew, and the next scheduled crew rotation to the ISS.

key_terms.definition: Russia's long-running spacecraft, in use since the 1960s, that ferries crews to and from the International Space Station.

stories.the_lesson: Even when two countries are at odds elsewhere, narrow, high-value areas of cooperation — like keeping a shared space station running — can keep functioning, because mutual benefit can outlast political friction when both sides need the arrangement to work.

stories.title: Pakistan-administered Kashmir votes under heavy security after a summer of deadly protests
key_points: Voting opened Monday in the first of **three rounds** of local elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir (AJK), under heavy security.
Nearly **30 people have been killed** since June in protests and clashes over the vote — even before polling day.
The anger centers on **12 assembly seats** reserved for Kashmiri refugees who fled to Pakistan after **1947 Partition** but no longer live in the region.
A political worker died in scuffles between rival party supporters in Kotli district as voting got under way Monday.
About **3.8 million residents** are eligible to vote across the Pakistan-controlled part of the disputed Himalayan territory.
stories.background: Kashmir has been split and disputed between India and Pakistan since Partition in 1947, with Pakistan administering one slice — Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) — while India controls Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh; both countries claim the whole region, and China holds a smaller sliver. AJK holds its own local legislative elections roughly every five years, separate from Pakistan's national polls, to choose a government responsible for local administration while Islamabad keeps control of defence and foreign affairs. Long-simmering anger over how power and representation are shared — especially the seats reserved for Kashmiri refugee-descendants who no longer live in AJK — boiled into open protest this summer.
stories.what_happened: Pakistan-administered Kashmir opened voting Monday in the first of three staggered rounds of local legislative elections, held under heavy security after a summer marked by violence. Protests demanding electoral reform escalated into deadly clashes, and even conservative counts put the death toll since early June at close to **30 people**, including protesters and law enforcement personnel. As polls opened, a political worker died in a scuffle between rival party supporters in the Kotli district's Nakyal area, and internet blackouts and roadblocks have periodically cut off parts of the region ahead of the vote. At the center of the unrest are **12 of the assembly's seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees** who resettled in Pakistan proper after the 1947 partition — protesters argue those seats should instead go to people who actually live in AJK today. Roughly 3.8 million residents are registered to vote in this first round, which covers the Mirpur division's 13 constituencies.
stories.why_it_matters: How this election plays out will shape who governs a territory that sits at the center of one of the world's longest-running territorial disputes, and a badly marred vote could deepen instability right on the India-Pakistan fault line. The refugee-seat dispute also raises a bigger question about who gets to decide Kashmir's future — those living there now, or a wider Pakistani-Kashmiri diaspora.
stories.ripple_effects: Continued unrest could strain Pakistan's already-stretched security forces and give India ammunition to question Pakistan's governance of the territory it claims. A contested or violent result could also fuel further protests and harder security crackdowns in the two remaining voting rounds.
stories.why_now: The vote was already scheduled for this summer, but the reform protests that erupted in June turned what would have been a routine local election into the most violent AJK vote in years, escalating right up to polling day.
stories.watch_next: Whether the remaining two rounds of voting go ahead peacefully, and whether the refugee-seat allocation becomes a flashpoint in the incoming assembly.

key_terms.definition: The part of the disputed Kashmir region administered by Pakistan, with its own local government but no independent foreign or defence policy.
The de facto military border dividing Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir since a 1972 ceasefire agreement.

stories.the_lesson: When an election's rules about who gets to vote or hold a seat are seen as unfair, the fight over those rules can become more explosive than the outcome itself — process disputes are often the real trigger behind political violence, not just who wins.

stories.title: China's Moonshot AI releases Kimi K3, the largest open-weight AI model ever built
key_points: Kimi K3 has **2.8 trillion parameters**, making it the largest open-weight AI model released to date.
Moonshot AI shipped the free download **a day early**, at roughly 7:30pm EDT on July 26.
It only activates a fraction of its parameters per request (a 'mixture-of-experts' design), keeping running costs down despite its size.
It ranks **fourth overall** on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, just behind Claude and GPT's top models but ahead of several others.
Moonshot is charging **roughly half** what Anthropic charges for its priciest model, undercutting Western rivals on price.
stories.background: 'Open-weight' models are AI systems whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, unlike 'closed' models such as those from OpenAI or Anthropic, which are only accessible through a paid API. Chinese AI labs, including Moonshot AI, have leaned into open-weight releases partly because **U.S. export controls limit their access to the most advanced computer chips**, making it harder to compete purely on raw compute — so they compete on giving the model away and letting the ecosystem build on it instead. Moonshot's prior model, Kimi K2.6, was already a well-regarded open-weight system; K3 is a major step up in scale.
stories.what_happened: Beijing-based Moonshot AI released the open weights for **Kimi K3**, a **2.8-trillion-parameter** AI model, making it downloadable for free roughly **a day earlier** than the company's own July 27 target. The model uses a 'sparse mixture-of-experts' design, meaning it only activates a small slice of its total parameters for any given task, which keeps inference costs down compared to a dense model of the same size. It supports a **1-million-token context window**, letting it process entire codebases or large document sets in a single pass. On independent benchmarks, K3 ranked behind only Anthropic's and OpenAI's top models on general intelligence, while beating other rivals, including Anthropic's Opus-tier model, on coding and agentic tasks specifically. Moonshot priced API access at **$3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens** — the highest of any Chinese lab, but still roughly half the cost of Anthropic's premium model for comparable work.
stories.why_it_matters: This is the largest open-weight AI model ever released, and it narrows the performance gap with the best closed, paid models from U.S. labs — while being cheaper and freely downloadable. That combination matters for any company or developer deciding which AI model to build on.
stories.ripple_effects: Cheaper, high-performing open-weight models put pricing pressure on the closed-model leaders (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google), and give companies in China and elsewhere a credible, low-cost alternative that doesn't depend on cutting-edge U.S.-controlled chips to run inference at scale. It also strengthens China's position in the global AI race despite chip export restrictions.
stories.why_now: Moonshot moved its own release date up by a day, shipping K3 on July 26 instead of the previously announced July 27 — a sign the company wanted to be first to market with a 3-trillion-parameter-class open model.
stories.watch_next: Whether U.S. labs respond with price cuts or a faster release cadence, and how quickly developers adopt K3 given its hardware demands.

key_terms.definition: An AI model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run themselves, instead of being locked behind a paid company API.
A model design where only a subset of the model's total parameters are used for any single request, cutting compute costs while keeping a very large total model size.

stories.the_lesson: When a country or company is restricted from the best hardware, one workaround is to compete on openness and price instead of raw scale — giving a model away for free can win market share even against a technically superior paid rival.
stories.market_link: Adds competitive pressure on Nvidia's biggest AI customers and on Western AI labs' pricing power; watch chipmakers and AI-infrastructure stocks for reaction.

stories.title: Wildfires force over 360,000 to flee France and Spain as Macron calls an emergency meeting

thread.previously: We reported Spain's wildfire death toll had climbed to 14 for the month, with 10 people still missing, as fires burned across the country.
thread.changed: The evacuation count has surged past **360,000 people** across France and Spain combined — one of the largest evacuations in French history — and French President Emmanuel Macron has called a crisis cabinet meeting today as a fresh heatwave threatens to make things worse.

key_points: More than **360,000 people** have now been evacuated across France and Spain combined.
The fire started in France's **Gironde region** last Wednesday before spreading into Spain.
It has burned roughly **104,000 acres in France** and **190,000 acres** around Avila and Toledo in Spain.
France has deployed **2,500 firefighters, 1,500 soldiers, and 1,200 police** to fight the blazes.
A **new heatwave** with temperatures near **40°C (104°F)** is forecast to hit the region this week.
stories.background: Southwestern Europe has been battling an unusually severe wildfire season this July, driven by a prolonged heatwave and tinder-dry vegetation after weeks of little rain. The fires began in France's Gironde wine region — the same area hit by major fires in 2022 — before winds pushed the blaze across the border into Spain's Castile and León and Madrid regions. Spain's death toll from this month's fires already stood at **14**, with **10 people still missing**, before this latest evacuation surge. Emergency services across both countries have been stretched thin fighting fires simultaneously on multiple fronts.
stories.what_happened: Wildfires that started in France's Gironde region last Wednesday have now forced more than **360,000 people** to evacuate their homes across France and Spain — one of the largest evacuations in French history. The fire has burned nearly **104,000 acres** in southwestern France and around **190,000 acres** in the Avila and Toledo areas west of Madrid. France has mobilized **2,500 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel, and roughly 1,200 police officers** to contain the blazes. French President **Emmanuel Macron** is holding a crisis cabinet meeting today, while Spanish Prime Minister **Pedro Sánchez** is visiting fire-hit areas in Valencia. Forecasters warn a fresh heatwave pushing temperatures to **40°C (104°F)** or higher is due to arrive this week, which could further complicate firefighting efforts.
stories.why_it_matters: This is now one of the largest civilian evacuations in recent French history, and it's unfolding while the fires are still actively spreading rather than winding down. The combination of ongoing fires and an incoming heatwave raises the risk that containment lines firefighters have built could fail.
stories.ripple_effects: Tourism-dependent regions in southwestern France and central Spain face major economic disruption during peak summer season. Insurers face a growing bill for destroyed homes and vineyards, and European governments are under renewed pressure to fund climate adaptation and firefighting capacity as these events become more frequent.
stories.why_now: A fresh heatwave arriving this week, on top of fires that have burned for nearly a week, has pushed both governments to escalate their response — hence Macron's crisis meeting and Sánchez's site visit today.
stories.watch_next: Whether firefighters can contain the blazes before the new 40°C heatwave arrives this week, and whether the missing-persons count in Spain changes.

key_terms.definition: An emergency gathering of a country's top government ministers to coordinate an urgent response, called when a situation is serious enough to need decisions above the level of individual agencies.

stories.the_lesson: Wildfires rarely respect borders — when conditions are right (heat, dry vegetation, wind), a single ignition can force evacuations across an entire region and overwhelm the emergency services of more than one country at once.
stories.market_link: Insurers with exposure to French and Spanish property, and European utilities/reinsurers, can see claims estimates move on days like this.

stories.title: Oil prices sink nearly 7% as the US-Iran ceasefire holds and Tehran opens Strait of Hormuz talks
key_points: **Brent crude fell 7.3%** to around **$89.73 a barrel**; **US WTI crude dropped 6.5%** to about **$83.47**.
The trigger is a holding pause in US-Iran hostilities, with Tehran now talking to Oman about the **Strait of Hormuz**.
Oil had surged **almost 40% this month** as fighting spread from the Strait of Hormuz toward the Red Sea shipping route.
World stock markets broadly **rose** on the news, even as some individual sectors (like chips) sold off separately.
stories.background: Earlier in July, the US carried out two weeks of nightly airstrikes on Iran before halting them; Iran responded in kind, and the ceasefire has held into this week. Oil markets had been pricing in serious disruption risk because Iran sits on the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow waterway that roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through daily — any Iranian move to block or mine it would choke off a huge share of global supply. That fear, plus fighting that spilled into Red Sea shipping lanes, drove crude up nearly 40% this month.
stories.what_happened: Crude oil futures dropped sharply on Monday as the ceasefire between the US and Iran continued to hold and Tehran reportedly opened talks with Oman over safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz. **Brent crude for September delivery fell 7.3% to roughly $89.73 a barrel**, while **US WTI crude fell 6.5% to about $83.47**. The move reverses a big chunk of this month's spike, which had been driven by fears that fighting could spread and choke off the Strait or the Red Sea route Saudi Arabia increasingly uses to move crude. Global stock markets rose on the relief, even as US chip stocks separately sold off for unrelated reasons.
stories.why_it_matters: Oil is the input cost behind almost everything — transport, plastics, fertilizer, electricity in many countries — so a swing this size moves inflation expectations, central bank calculations, and household budgets worldwide almost overnight.
stories.ripple_effects: Cheaper oil eases pressure on countries like India that import most of their crude (which is part of why India's own stock market jumped on the same news), and it takes some heat off central banks worried about energy-driven inflation. But it also cuts revenue for oil exporters and could reduce the incentive for Iran to keep the ceasefire if oil-related leverage was part of its calculus.
stories.why_now: This is a direct market reaction to the ceasefire holding through the weekend and the new Iran-Oman talks over the Strait — traders had been pricing in a worse outcome.
stories.watch_next: Whether the Iran-Oman Strait of Hormuz talks produce a concrete agreement, which would further cement the price relief; a collapse of the ceasefire would send oil sharply back up.

key_terms.definition: A narrow shipping channel between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply passes through — the single most important chokepoint in global energy markets.
The two main global oil price benchmarks — Brent tracks international oil (mostly from the North Sea), WTI tracks US oil.

stories.the_lesson: Oil prices react less to actual supply changes than to the *risk* of supply changes — a credible ceasefire can erase a price spike almost as fast as the conflict that caused it.
stories.market_link: Airlines and shipping benefit from lower fuel costs; oil majors and energy-exporter currencies (like the Russian ruble or Gulf currencies) face pressure; India's Sensex and the rupee both got a lift from the same move.

stories.title: Israel's West Bank crackdown widens to 300+ raided sites as Palestinians say they're nearing 'breaking point'
key_points: Israeli forces have searched **more than 300 locations** across the West Bank since Friday's deadly clash.
The trigger: a shootout near the village of Tal killed **four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers** on July 24.
Over **70 Palestinians** have been detained, with troops raiding roughly **70 homes** in Tal alone.
The UN says **68 Palestinians** have been killed in the West Bank in 2026 so far, at least 13 by settlers.
Settlers have grown bolder alongside the military operation, attempting to **torch two mosques**.
stories.background: The West Bank is Palestinian territory that Israel has militarily occupied since 1967; roughly 500,000 Israeli settlers now live there alongside about 3 million Palestinians, and settler-Palestinian friction has been rising for years. On July 24, a confrontation broke out near the village of Tal, southwest of Nablus, after settlers raided the town — a Palestinian grabbed a security officer's weapon and a shootout followed, leaving **four Palestinians (from one family) and two Israeli soldiers dead**. Prime Minister **Netanyahu ordered a 'wide-scale military operation'** in response, which has intensified daily since.
stories.what_happened: Israeli troops have spent the weekend and into Monday sweeping the West Bank: raiding more than **300 locations**, searching for what the military calls Hamas affiliates, arms traffickers and other suspected militants. In Tal itself, soldiers raided about 70 homes and detained roughly 50 people, sealing the house of the Palestinian involved in Friday's shooting. Detentions have spread well beyond Tal — to Jenin, Tubas, the Al-Far'a refugee camp, Ramallah, Al-Bireh and Hebron — with more than 70 people held in total. Troops also raided a hospital in Nablus as part of the operation. Alongside the military sweep, Jewish settlers have grown more aggressive, marauding through villages, spray-painting graffiti, and attempting to set two mosques on fire. By Monday, Palestinian residents were telling reporters the pressure from both settlers and soldiers was pushing the area toward a 'breaking point.'
stories.why_it_matters: This is one of the most intense Israeli military operations inside the West Bank in years, arriving while Israel is already stretched by the broader Iran confrontation. A rising Palestinian death toll and mass detentions raise the risk of a bigger explosion of violence in a territory that, unlike Gaza, sits in the middle of Israel's own security perimeter.
stories.ripple_effects: Escalation here complicates the diplomacy Netanyahu is doing simultaneously in Washington (he is due at the White House this week) and could draw international criticism at a moment the US is trying to broker calm across the region. It also hardens positions on both sides ahead of any future ceasefire or statehood talks, and increases pressure on Arab governments that have been normalizing ties with Israel.
stories.why_now: The July 24 shootout near Tal was the spark, but it landed on top of months of rising settler violence that the UN and rights groups had already flagged as approaching crisis levels.
stories.watch_next: Whether Netanyahu's operation formally expands or scales back once he returns from his Washington trip this week.

key_terms.definition: A landlocked Palestinian territory between Israel and Jordan that Israel has occupied militarily since the 1967 war; part of it is administered by the Palestinian Authority.
Israeli civilians who live in communities built in the occupied West Bank, considered illegal under international law by most of the world, though Israel disputes this.

stories.the_lesson: When a single deadly incident lands on top of a slow-building grievance, the response is rarely proportionate to the trigger alone — it reflects months of accumulated tension finally breaking through.

stories.title: German prosecutors confirm the Berlin Pride attack was Islamist terrorism and lay out the attacker's fuller radicalization timeline
key_points: Prosecutors formally confirmed the van-and-blade attack at Berlin's Pride festival was an **Islamist terror attack**, not just a suspected one
Attacker **Abdul Ballout, 21,** had tried to join ISIS in 2025 — he traveled to Lebanon, was arrested there, and served **three months** in a Lebanese military prison
Back in Germany, he received a suspended sentence of **1 year and 10 months** for preparing a serious act of violence — meaning he was free to carry out Saturday's attack
He also had a **2022 juvenile conviction** for assault and robbery, showing a longer pattern authorities had already flagged
The disclosures sharpen questions about why someone twice-convicted for violence-linked offenses was still free to act
stories.background: A van rammed a crowd near Berlin's Pride festival on Saturday night, killing one woman and injuring 29 people, before the driver fled and was shot dead by police roughly 20 hours later in a manhunt. Germany's interior minister called it a suspected Islamist terror attack within hours, and authorities quickly named the driver as **Abdul Ballout**, a German citizen of Lebanese descent — but the full picture of his background was still emerging. Germany has faced a string of vehicle-ramming and knife attacks tied to Islamist extremism in recent years, repeatedly raising the question of how radicalized individuals already known to police still manage to act.
stories.what_happened: German federal prosecutors on Monday laid out the fullest account yet of Ballout's path to the attack. He shared ISIS propaganda online in **2024**, then traveled to Lebanon in **2025** intending to cross into Syria and join the group; Lebanese authorities arrested him and a military court sentenced him to **three months in prison** there. Back in Germany, he was convicted of preparing a serious act of subversive violence but received a **suspended sentence of one year and ten months** — partly because of time already served in Lebanon and partly because he told the court he had distanced himself from ISIS. Prosecutors also confirmed a **2022 juvenile conviction** for assault and robbery, filling in a longer history of run-ins with the law before Saturday's attack.
stories.why_it_matters: The new details turn a fast-moving breaking story into a pointed accountability question: how did a young man with two prior convictions — one explicitly tied to attempted ISIS involvement — remain free to carry out a deadly attack? That's now a direct test of Germany's approach to monitoring and sentencing people flagged for extremism risk.
stories.ripple_effects: Expect German politicians to face pressure over deradicalization policy and sentencing guidelines for extremism-linked offenses, alongside renewed debate over migration and integration policy. Security planning for large public events across Germany and Europe is likely to tighten further this summer as a result.
stories.why_now: Prosecutors released the fuller timeline today as the formal investigation caught up with the fast-moving weekend events — the attack, manhunt, and shooting all happened within about 24 hours, before authorities had assembled the complete background.
stories.watch_next: Watch for whether Chancellor Merz's government proposes concrete changes to how convicted extremism-risk individuals are monitored or sentenced.

key_terms.definition: A prison sentence a court formally hands down but does not require the person to actually serve, usually on the condition they don't reoffend — meaning the person stays free.

stories.the_lesson: A criminal conviction on paper doesn't automatically mean a dangerous person is off the streets — suspended sentences and time-served credits can leave someone free despite a documented history of violence-linked offenses.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported a van rammed a Pride festival crowd in Berlin, killing one woman and injuring 29; the suspect, Abdul Ballout, fled and was shot dead by police about 20 hours later, with Germany's interior minister calling it a suspected Islamist terror attack and noting Ballout had a prior suspended conviction tied to Islamic State propaganda.
thread.changed: Prosecutors have now formally confirmed the Islamist terror motive and released the fuller timeline: Ballout's 2025 attempt to join ISIS via Lebanon, his three months in a Lebanese military prison, the exact length of his suspended German sentence (1 year 10 months), and a previously-undisclosed 2022 juvenile conviction for assault and robbery.
